items.definition: doing what a person in authority tells you to do
items.example: Our first subject is obedience.

items.definition: a person who offers to take part in something without being forced
items.example: You are a volunteer for a study of memory.

items.definition: accepted as having the right to give orders or make decisions
items.example: Yale is a famous and legitimate institution.

items.definition: a person who secretly works with the researcher while pretending to be an ordinary participant
items.example: In fact he is a confederate: an actor who works for the experimenter.

items.definition: to pause before you do something because you are not sure
items.example: If you hesitate, the experimenter answers with a prod.

items.definition: a short push; here, a standard sentence that tells someone to go on
items.example: The experimenter answers with a prod.

items.definition: strong feelings of worry, pain or unhappiness
items.example: Many volunteers showed clear distress.

items.definition: making someone believe something that is not true
items.example: The whole study relied on deception.

items.definition: a fixed series of actions that are done in a particular order
items.example: Forty men took part in a procedure at Yale.

items.definition: the result of something
items.example: The outcome was far higher than the experts had predicted.

items.definition: to do what you are told or asked to do
items.example: Ordinary people may comply with an authority.

items.definition: worried and upset
items.example: Many volunteers were visibly troubled.

items.definition: good enough to be allowed
items.example: Was the research itself acceptable?

items.definition: to vary between a lowest and a highest value
items.example: The share ranged from 28 to 91 per cent.

items.definition: normal or usual for a kind of thing
items.example: Harm that is more typical of modern life.

items.definition: doubting whether something is true or good
items.example: Be sceptical of the headline and of its critics.

items.definition: the health, safety and happiness of a person or group
items.example: Her main objection was about the volunteers' welfare.

items.definition: a person's agreement to take part after being told honestly what will happen
items.example: They had not given real informed consent.

items.definition: to explain the true purpose of a study to participants after it has finished
items.example: Every volunteer was told the truth in a debrief.

items.definition: a request that speaks to a person's values or feelings
items.example: Appeals to the value of science worked better than orders.

items.definition: a collection of old documents and records
items.example: A third kind of criticism came from the archive.

items.definition: a public argument about something that people strongly disagree about
items.example: Here is a summary of the ethical controversy.

items.definition: an explanation of what something means
items.example: The second objection is about interpretation.

items.definition: a group of people chosen to make decisions or give advice
items.example: Research ethics committees became routine.

items.definition: to make something no longer valid or true
items.example: Neither objection cancels the study.

items.definition: to feel that you share the aims or feelings of a person or group
items.example: The volunteers identified with the scientific cause.

items.definition: to perform or organise something again
items.example: They restaged the procedure for a film.

items.definition: complicated and not clear or tidy
items.example: The archive tells a messier story.

items.definition: a version of a procedure in which one thing is changed
items.example: Milgram ran about twenty variations of the study.

items.definition: a rule or measure that protects people from harm
items.example: Stopping at 150 volts was a reasonable safeguard.

items.definition: statistically significant: unlikely to be caused by chance alone
items.example: The difference was not statistically significant.

items.definition: a new study that repeats an earlier study to check its result
items.example: This is a partial replication.

items.definition: a warning that a statement is only true under certain conditions
items.example: Every claim needs a caveat.

items.definition: a statement that something is true, especially one that is not yet proved
items.example: Let us test some claims.

items.definition: strong and not easily broken or disproved
items.example: The finding appears robust in a limited sense.

items.definition: to say that something is true for a whole group or for all situations
items.example: The finding cannot be generalised without caution.

items.definition: belonging to the present time
items.example: The result is contemporary as well as historical.

items.definition: to stay in the same state or place
items.example: Three things seem to remain.

items.definition: to get the same result again by repeating a study
items.example: Can the result be reproduced?

items.definition: connected with what is morally right
items.example: Researchers now use ethical designs.

items.text: What do you say to the experimenter?
items.example: What do you say to the experimenter? I'm not comfortable going on. I would like to stop now.
items.qaAnswer: I'm not comfortable going on. I would like to stop now.
qaWrong: I no want continue more.
Stop this at once! You are a monster!

items.text: Results paragraph: which sentence reports it correctly?
items.example: Results paragraph: which sentence reports it correctly? Every volunteer reached 300 volts, and 26 of the 40 (65 per cent) continued to the maximum.
items.qaAnswer: Every volunteer reached 300 volts, and 26 of the 40 (65 per cent) continued to the maximum.
qaWrong: All forty volunteers went on to the maximum, 450 volts.
The outcome were higher than the experts predicted.

items.text: Which version is the most careful and accurate?
items.example: Which version is the most careful and accurate? The results suggest that many ordinary people may keep following instructions even when this causes serious distress to someone else.
items.qaAnswer: The results suggest that many ordinary people may keep following instructions even when this causes serious distress to someone else.
qaWrong: The study proves that everybody is a potential torturer.
The results suggest that many people tends to obey authority.

items.text: Which sentence reports Milgram's reply to Baumrind correctly?
items.example: Which sentence reports Milgram's reply to Baumrind correctly? Milgram replied that the stress had been unexpected and brief, and argued that the follow-up showed no lasting harm.
items.qaAnswer: Milgram replied that the stress had been unexpected and brief, and argued that the follow-up showed no lasting harm.
qaWrong: Milgram admitted that the volunteers had suffered lasting harm.
Milgram replying that the debriefing was protecting the volunteers.

items.text: What did Haslam, Reicher and Birney find in their analogue study?
items.example: What did Haslam, Reicher and Birney find in their analogue study? Appeals to the value of science were more effective than orders.
items.qaAnswer: Appeals to the value of science were more effective than orders.
qaWrong: Orders worked better than any other prod.
The prods had no effect at all.

items.text: Which version reports the criticism most carefully?
items.example: Which version reports the criticism most carefully? Some researchers argue that the volunteers were responding to appeals to science rather than to orders.
items.qaAnswer: Some researchers argue that the volunteers were responding to appeals to science rather than to orders.
qaWrong: The critics have proved that Milgram made up his results.
According to Perry, many volunteers doubts the shocks were real.

items.text: What do the variations in Milgram's study suggest?
items.example: What do the variations in Milgram's study suggest? That the situation strongly affects how far people go, and that support from others makes refusal much easier.
items.qaAnswer: That the situation strongly affects how far people go, and that support from others makes refusal much easier.
qaWrong: That obedience does not depend on the situation.
That the lab coat was the only thing that mattered.

items.text: Which sentence uses the evidence from the Discussion most carefully?
items.example: Which sentence uses the evidence from the Discussion most carefully? The replications suggest that the finding is robust, but it cannot be generalised to every situation.
items.qaAnswer: The replications suggest that the finding is robust, but it cannot be generalised to every situation.
qaWrong: The replications prove that people everywhere always obey.
The finding can be generalise to all situations.

items.text: Claim: "Ordinary people always obey authority." What is its status?
items.example: Claim: "Ordinary people always obey authority." What is its status? Too strong.
qaWrong: Still supported.
Completely disproved.

items.text: Claim: "Situations can push many people further than they expect." What is its status?
items.example: Claim: "Situations can push many people further than they expect." What is its status? Still supported, but "obedience" may be the wrong explanation.
items.qaAnswer: Still supported, but "obedience" may be the wrong explanation.
qaWrong: Too strong.
Completely disproved.
